title: Should fans own football clubs?
intro: Four writers comment on the idea of football clubs being owned by their supporters.

texts.author: Rachel Moss, sports economist
texts.text: The financial case for fan ownership is stronger than many people assume. Clubs run by their supporters tend to spend within their means, because members have no interest in gambling the club's future on a few expensive signings, and they are far less likely to end up in administration. That said, we should be honest about the limits of the model. At the very top of the game, where clubs compete for players with billionaire owners and sovereign wealth funds, a club funded by membership fees simply cannot keep up. For that reason, I believe the government has a role to play: clear rules on who may own a club, and on how much debt it can take on, would protect supporters far more effectively than relying on the goodwill of individual owners.

texts.author: Tom Hartley, football journalist
texts.text: Romantic as it sounds, fan ownership is usually a recipe for financial stagnation. Supporters' trusts rarely have the capital needed to improve stadiums or training facilities, and clubs that depend on them gradually fall behind their rivals. It is no coincidence that none of the continent's leading clubs is owned by its fans; they would struggle to attract the players needed to win major trophies. Nor do I accept that politicians should intervene. Football clubs are businesses, and if supporters dislike an owner, the market already gives them a voice: they can stop buying tickets. Talk of 'community identity' strikes me as largely sentimental; a club's bond with its town depends on its history and its results, not on who happens to hold the shares.

texts.author: Luis Ortega, former professional player
texts.text: Having played for clubs with very different owners, I can say that the fan-owned ones were by far the best run. Nobody was tempted to spend money the club did not have, and wages were always paid on time. People claim that such clubs can never succeed at the highest level, but I disagree. With good coaching and a clever approach to recruitment, a well-organised club can compete with anyone, at least for a few seasons, and history offers more examples than the sceptics admit. What impressed me most, though, was the atmosphere. When supporters own the club, they treat it as part of the town's identity, and the players feel that connection every time they walk onto the pitch.

texts.author: Amira Khan, supporters' representative
texts.text: Our members do not expect to win the Champions League. We know that, in today's game, a club owned by its fans cannot realistically challenge the wealthiest clubs in Europe, and we have made our peace with that. What we refuse to accept is the idea that supporters should simply hope for a responsible owner. Too many clubs have been pushed to the brink of collapse by owners who treated them as playthings, and only legislation can prevent that from happening again. In any case, the benefits of fan ownership are not mainly about trophies. Since our members took over, the club has become a meeting point for the whole town: volunteers run the youth teams, and children in the area wear our shirt rather than those of distant giants.

items.question: Which writer shares writer A's view on the financial effects of fan ownership?
items.hint: A thinks fan-owned clubs are financially more careful. Who else praises how they are run?
items.explanation: C says fan-owned clubs were 'by far the best run' and never spent money they did not have, like A. B thinks fan ownership leads to 'financial stagnation'; D does not discuss the club's finances.

items.question: Which writer has a different opinion from the others on whether fan-owned clubs can compete at the highest level?
items.hint: Three writers think fan-owned clubs cannot compete with the richest clubs. Who disagrees?
items.explanation: C says a well-organised fan-owned club 'can compete with anyone'. A, B and D all believe such clubs cannot keep up with the wealthiest ones.

items.question: Which writer expresses a similar view to writer A regarding the need for government involvement?
items.hint: A wants clear rules from the government. Who else talks about legislation?
items.explanation: D says 'only legislation can prevent' irresponsible owners from ruining clubs, like A. B rejects political intervention, and C does not mention it.

items.question: Which writer, like writer C, believes that fan ownership strengthens a club's connection with its local community?
items.hint: C talks about the town's identity. Who describes the club becoming part of town life?
items.explanation: D says the club has become 'a meeting point for the whole town'. B dismisses talk of community identity as 'sentimental', and A does not discuss it.

title: Is homework worth it?
intro: Four people with an interest in education give their views on homework.

texts.author: Sarah Whitfield, secondary school teacher
texts.text: In my experience, homework does help older students to learn, provided it consolidates what was taught in class rather than introducing new material. A short exercise the same evening can make the difference between understanding a topic and forgetting it by the next lesson. However, I have seen at first hand the toll that excessive homework takes on families. Evenings become a battleground, and parents who work long hours feel guilty that they cannot help. For pupils at primary school, I would scrap it altogether. Young children learn far more from playing, reading for pleasure and simply talking to the adults around them than from worksheets, and the habit of independent study can wait until secondary school.

texts.author: Martin Leclerc, education researcher
texts.text: The evidence that homework improves learning is far weaker than most people imagine. Studies that report benefits tend to find small effects, and many of them cannot rule out the possibility that motivated students simply do more homework. I am equally sceptical, however, of the claim that homework is ruining family life. Surveys suggest that most families spend less than half an hour a day on it, and the stories of tearful children working until midnight are the exception rather than the rule. My own conclusion is that homework for primary pupils should be dropped, since the time could be better spent elsewhere. As for online homework, it has made it easier than ever for students to copy answers or let an app do the work.

texts.author: Jenny Ahmed, parent
texts.text: My two children have homework most evenings, and I am convinced it does them good. It teaches them to organise their time and to keep practising things like spelling and times tables, which they would otherwise forget. I won't pretend it is always easy: there are evenings when everyone ends up shouting, and weekends when it feels as if homework has taken over the house. Even so, I would be strongly against abolishing it for younger children, because I believe good habits need to start early. One thing that has helped enormously is the online platform the school now uses. The children get instant feedback on their answers, and I can see at a glance what they have done.

texts.author: Graham Price, headteacher
texts.text: Well-designed homework undoubtedly helps students learn; the problem is that not all homework is well designed. In some schools, pupils receive several hours a week of tasks that are set because parents expect them, not because they serve any purpose, and the resulting pressure on families is real. We have responded by setting less homework but making it more focused. Online platforms have been a great help in this respect. Teachers spend less time marking, students receive feedback immediately rather than a week later, and we can see which questions caused problems before the next lesson. I would encourage any school that has not yet tried them to do so.

items.question: Which writer has a different opinion from the others about the effect homework has on family life?
items.hint: Three writers describe homework causing stress at home. Who thinks this is exaggerated?
items.explanation: B says stories of homework ruining family life are 'the exception rather than the rule'. A, C and D all describe real pressure on families.

items.question: Which writer shares writer B's view that homework should be abolished for younger children?
items.hint: B wants to drop homework for primary pupils. Who would 'scrap it altogether'?
items.explanation: A would 'scrap it altogether' for primary pupils, like B. C is strongly against abolishing it, and D does not discuss younger children.

items.question: Which writer expresses a similar view to writer C on the value of online homework platforms?
items.hint: C praises the instant feedback of an online platform. Who else is positive about online platforms?
items.explanation: D says online platforms have been 'a great help', with immediate feedback, like C. B thinks online homework makes cheating easier, and A does not mention it.

items.question: Which writer has a different view from writer A on whether homework helps students learn?
items.hint: A thinks homework helps older students learn. Who doubts that it improves learning?
items.explanation: B says the evidence that homework improves learning is 'far weaker than most people imagine'. C and D, like A, believe it helps.

title: Social media and democracy
topic: the effect of social media on politics
intro: Four writers consider whether social media is good for democracy.

texts.author: Helena Sørensen, political scientist
texts.text: Whatever its faults, social media has drawn a generation of young people into politics who would otherwise have ignored it. Campaigns that began as hashtags have led to real changes in the law, and turnout among first-time voters has risen in several countries. The spread of false information is a genuine threat, but it is naive to expect the platforms to deal with it themselves when their profits depend on attention; only legislation will change their behaviour. I am less worried than many commentators about so-called echo chambers. Research suggests that most users actually come across a wider range of opinions online than they do in their daily lives, even if they do not always enjoy the experience.

texts.author: Owen Clarke, journalist
texts.text: We should not confuse clicking 'like' with taking part in politics. Social media has made it easy to feel involved without doing anything that changes the outcome of an election, and I see little evidence that young people are more engaged than before. Meanwhile, misinformation spreads faster than any correction, and governments must force the platforms to take responsibility for what they publish. The algorithms make matters worse by showing users more of what they already believe, until each group lives in its own version of reality. One simple reform would help: requiring people to post under their real names. Much of the cruelty and dishonesty online depends on the protection that anonymity provides.

texts.author: Priya Raman, technology entrepreneur
texts.text: Social media is the most powerful tool for political participation ever invented. Young people who would never join a party now organise campaigns, question politicians directly and share information instantly. Of course misinformation exists, but the platforms have every incentive to tackle it, and they are developing far more sophisticated methods than any government regulator could design. Heavy-handed laws would simply stifle innovation. I do accept that recommendation algorithms can trap users in bubbles of like-minded people, and that is something the industry needs to address. What we must not do is end anonymity. For whistle-blowers and people living under repressive governments, the ability to speak without revealing their identity can be a matter of life and death.

texts.author: Kwame Mensah, sociologist
texts.text: My research with students suggests that social media has genuinely increased their interest in political issues, particularly the environment and housing. That is good news. The bad news is that the same platforms make it easy to spread lies, and experience shows that voluntary codes of conduct achieve very little; clear legal obligations are needed. On the other hand, I think the fear of echo chambers has been overstated. Most people's feeds contain a surprising mix of views, not least because they follow friends and relatives who disagree with them. I would also defend the right to anonymity. It protects many people, from teenagers exploring their identity to employees reporting wrongdoing, whose voices might otherwise never be heard.

items.question: Which writer has a different opinion from the others on whether social media has increased young people's involvement in politics?
items.hint: Three writers think young people are more politically involved. Who says 'liking' is not taking part?
items.explanation: B sees 'little evidence that young people are more engaged than before'. A, C and D all believe social media has increased their involvement.

items.question: Which writer takes a different view from the others on how the problem of misinformation should be dealt with?
items.hint: Three writers want laws. Who trusts the platforms to solve it?
items.explanation: C believes the platforms can tackle misinformation themselves and that laws would 'stifle innovation'. A, B and D all call for legislation.

items.question: Which writer shares writer A's opinion about echo chambers?
items.hint: A thinks the danger of echo chambers is exaggerated. Who else says the fear is 'overstated'?
items.explanation: D says the fear of echo chambers 'has been overstated', like A. B and C both think algorithms do trap users in bubbles.

items.question: Which writer, like writer D, thinks that people should be allowed to remain anonymous online?
items.hint: D defends anonymity. Who else says 'we must not end anonymity'?
items.explanation: C says 'What we must not do is end anonymity', like D. B wants people to post under their real names, and A does not discuss anonymity.

title: Car-free city centres
intro: Four people give their views on removing cars from city centres.

texts.author: Sofia Bianchi, urban planner
texts.text: Every city that has removed cars from its centre has faced the same predictions of disaster, and they have almost never come true. Pedestrians linger, browse and return more often than drivers, so shops and cafés in car-free streets usually see their takings rise within a year or two. Nor should cities wait for perfect public transport before acting; it is the reduction in traffic itself that creates the demand for better buses and trams. The benefits for public health are considerable, too, with dramatic falls in air pollution recorded wherever schemes have been introduced. The one condition I would insist on is that disabled drivers and those who depend on a car to get around keep their right of access.

texts.author: Daniel Frost, shop owner
texts.text: My customers come from all over the region, and most of them drive. Since the council closed the high street to traffic, my turnover has fallen by a third, and three of my neighbours have already shut up shop. I have no doubt that the air is cleaner, and I would not want to go back to the traffic jams of ten years ago. But it is simply unfair to ban cars before there is a decent alternative. The buses that serve this area run once an hour and stop at eight in the evening. Improve those first, and people may well be happy to leave their cars at home; do it the other way round, and they will just shop elsewhere.

texts.author: Hannah Lee, environmental scientist
texts.text: Car-free centres are often presented as the answer to urban air pollution, but the reality is more complicated. Much of the pollution in our cities comes from heating, industry and traffic on the ring roads that surround the centre, so the measurable improvement is usually modest. That does not mean such schemes are a bad idea. Streets without cars are quieter, safer and more pleasant, and the evidence suggests that local businesses tend to do better, not worse. I also think it would be a mistake to delay until the transport network is perfect. Experience shows that bus and tram services improve fastest once politicians have a clear reason to invest in them.

texts.author: Marcus Webb, disability campaigner
texts.text: I am all in favour of cleaner, quieter cities, and nobody who has breathed the air on our busiest streets can doubt that removing traffic brings real health benefits. But too many car-free schemes are designed by people who walk and cycle easily. Before the cars go, there must be accessible public transport that actually serves the people who need it, with low-floor buses, step-free stations and services in the evening. Otherwise, people with limited mobility are effectively locked out of the city centre. And even with good transport, some disabled people will still need to drive or be driven to the door, so any ban must include clear exemptions for them.

items.question: Which writer disagrees with writer A about the effect of car-free centres on local businesses?
items.hint: A says shops do better without cars. Who says the opposite has happened?
items.explanation: B says his turnover has fallen by a third since the street was closed to traffic. C agrees with A that businesses do better, and D does not discuss shops.

items.question: Which writer has a different view from the others on how much car-free zones improve air quality?
items.hint: Three writers accept that the air gets much cleaner. Who says the improvement is 'modest'?
items.explanation: C says the measurable improvement is 'usually modest' because most pollution comes from elsewhere. A, B and D all accept clear benefits for the air.

items.question: Which writer shares writer B's view that public transport must be improved before cars are banned?
items.hint: B says 'Improve those first'. Who says 'Before the cars go, there must be…'?
items.explanation: D insists that accessible public transport must exist 'before the cars go', like B. A and C both argue that cities should not wait for transport to improve.

items.question: Which writer, like writer D, insists that exceptions must be made for people with limited mobility?
items.hint: D wants clear exemptions for disabled people. Who else sets this as a condition?
items.explanation: A's 'one condition' is that disabled drivers keep their right of access, like D. B and C do not discuss exemptions.
